concepts.def: Each planet orbits the Sun in an ellipse with the Sun at one focus, so its distance from the Sun varies through the orbit.
A line joining a planet to the Sun sweeps out equal areas in equal times, so the planet moves faster when nearer the Sun at perihelion.
The square of a planet's orbital period is proportional to the cube of its semi-major axis (T squared proportional to a cubed) for bodies orbiting the Sun.
Every mass attracts every other with a force proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of their separation.
A measure of how elongated an orbit is; a value of 0 is a perfect circle while values nearer 1 describe increasingly stretched ellipses.
The difference in gravitational pull across a body, mainly from the Moon, which raises two tidal bulges on Earth and drives the cycle of tides.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Solar System Dynamics — a core area of A-Level Astronomy.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Solar System Dynamics brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Solar System Dynamics.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Kepler's First Law states that planetary orbits are:
options: Perfect circles
Ellipses with the Sun at one focus
Spirals
Straight lines

mcqs.q: A planet moves fastest in its orbit when it is:
options: Farthest from the Sun
Closest to the Sun (perihelion)
At constant speed throughout
At aphelion

mcqs.q: Newton's law of gravitation says the force varies with separation as:
options: Proportional to distance
Inversely with the square of distance
Inversely with distance
Proportional to distance squared

mcqs.q: An orbit with an eccentricity of 0 is:
options: A parabola
A perfect circle
A highly stretched ellipse
An escape path
Its mass increases near the Sun.
No - they are ellipses with the Sun at one focus (Kepler's First Law).
They are spirals slowly winding inward.
Yes, all orbits are circular.

mcqs.q: Why does a planet speed up near the Sun?
options: The Sun's heat pushes it along faster.
The Earth's rotation acting alone.
It sweeps equal areas in equal times, so it must move faster at perihelion.
Its mass increases near the Sun.

mcqs.q: What mainly causes Earth's ocean tides?
options: They are spirals slowly winding inward.
The Sun's heat boiling the sea.
The Earth's rotation acting alone.
The Moon's gravitational pull, which varies across the Earth.
